mcqs.question: What's a concrete test for whether an app's presentation, domain, and data layers are actually properly separated?
options: Whether the app has exactly three top-level folders named presentation, domain, and data
Whether the data layer's implementation can be swapped (e.g. mocked for tests) without changing any domain or presentation code
Whether each layer has the same number of files as the others
Whether the UI framework used is SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose rather than UIKit or Views
mcqs.explanation: The real test of layering is behavioral, not organizational — can a lower layer's implementation change without rippling into layers above it, which is exactly what dependency inversion behind an interface enables. Folder naming, file counts, and UI framework choice are unrelated to whether the actual dependency direction is enforced.

mcqs.question: A team says 'we use Clean Architecture for the app and MVI for our screens.' Is this a coherent combination?
options: No — Clean Architecture and MVI are mutually exclusive alternatives and cannot be combined
No — MVI can only be used with MVVM, never with Clean Architecture
Yes, but only if the app has fewer than ten screens total
Yes — Clean Architecture is a whole-app layering discipline, and MVI is a pattern for structuring state within the presentation layer; they answer different-scoped questions
mcqs.explanation: Clean Architecture addresses whole-app layering (presentation/domain/data) while MVI addresses how state is organized within one screen's presentation layer — they operate at different scopes and commonly pair together in real apps. Presenting them as mutually exclusive, or gating the combination on screen count, misunderstands what each actually governs.

mcqs.question: How does splitting an app into feature modules (checkout, profile, search) with enforced module visibility differ from just organizing code into packages within one module?
options: There is no real difference — both provide identical enforcement
Feature modules always run faster at runtime than package-organized code
Module boundaries are compiler-enforced, so another module genuinely cannot access another module's internals, unlike package organization which relies on convention
Package organization is only a valid approach for backend code, never for mobile apps
mcqs.explanation: The key structural difference is enforcement: a module's public interface is the only thing visible outside it, compiler-checked, while 'please don't import from that package' is an unenforced convention that erodes over time. Runtime performance isn't the distinguishing factor, and package organization is a valid mobile pattern too, just with weaker boundary guarantees.

mcqs.question: A repository's real job goes beyond simply fetching data from the network. What's the other key responsibility described here?
options: Rendering the UI for whatever data it fetches
Establishing one source of truth, typically the local database, that the UI reads from consistently while the repository keeps it synced with the network
Handling all user authentication for the app
Compiling the app's network requests into a single batched request per screen
mcqs.explanation: Beyond fetching, a repository's architectural value is providing one consistent source of truth for the UI to read from, typically the local database kept in sync with the network — this avoids the UI having to juggle 'is this the cached or the fresh network response' itself. Rendering UI, handling all authentication, and request batching are not the repository pattern's defining responsibility.

mcqs.question: Every feature module in an app imports one shared AppRepository class that has accumulated methods for every feature's data needs over two years. What's the architectural problem this creates?
options: It has no real downside as long as the class compiles without errors
The only issue is stylistic — the class should be renamed to something more descriptive
This pattern is required for Clean Architecture to work correctly
It couples every feature to every other feature transitively through the shared class, defeating the isolation modularization was meant to provide
mcqs.explanation: A God repository that every feature depends on directly reintroduces coupling between features through their shared dependency, undermining the isolation that splitting into feature modules was supposed to achieve — this is a structural problem, not a naming issue, and it's the opposite of what Clean Architecture's layering actually calls for.

mcqs.question: A discount-eligibility rule is written as an inline conditional directly inside a screen's view model. What's the concrete cost of this, beyond code style?
options: The rule cannot be unit-tested without instantiating the whole UI layer, and it can't be reused if another screen needs the same rule
The app will run measurably slower due to the inline conditional
The code will fail to compile since business logic is not permitted in a view model
There is no real cost — this is the correct place for business rules in any architecture
mcqs.explanation: The concrete costs are testability and reuse — a rule buried in a view model can't be tested in isolation from the UI layer and can't be shared if a second screen needs the identical logic, which is exactly what a domain-layer use case would solve. This isn't a compile error or a performance issue; it's a maintainability cost that compounds as the rule needs to change or be reused.
